strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in video anomaly detection: obtaining rare, sensitive abnormal footage. Training with generated anomalies rather than real abnormal videos is potentially impactful.

CA-PAG is a coherent pipeline combining CLIP-based seed-frame retrieval, image-conditioned video diffusion, and scene-aware prompt refinement. The qualitative examples include a useful failure case rather than showing only successful generations.

The detector-side study reports sizable gains from DARM over the same UR-DMU-based configuration: 96.0 to 98.2 AUC on ShanghaiTech and 80.2 to 82.5 on UCF-Crime. The component and synthetic-data-volume ablations provide some evidence that the gains are not solely due to adding more generated clips.

The paper evaluates on two established benchmarks, reports both spatial and temporal generation metrics, documents generation cost and many training hyperparameters, and acknowledges difficulty with long-horizon, context-dependent anomalies.
weaknesses: The experimental protocol does not support several headline comparisons. PA-VAD is given the names of all anomaly classes expected at inference, while conventional unsupervised VAD baselines receive neither abnormal videos nor this test-category supervision. Calling these settings 'fully fair' and claiming state-of-the-art UVAD performance is therefore misleading. Conversely, comparison with weakly supervised methods is also not controlled for backbone, feature extractor, augmentation, or supervision.

The strongest claim relies on a 0.6-point ShanghaiTech improvement over a real-abnormal method, but there are no multiple-run statistics, confidence intervals, or controlled reimplementations. Results are reported on only two benchmarks, and the method remains substantially below real-abnormal methods on UCF-Crime. Per-class results are especially important for a class-aware generator but are absent.

Critical methodological details are missing. DARM requires 50/80 generated pseudo-normal clips, yet the manuscript never explains how these clips are generated. The usage-aware 'update' is presented only as a loss, without specifying detachment, optimization order, or safeguards against prototype/feature collapse. Several necessary values and procedures, including retrieval K, balancing parameters, lambda in retrieval, tau, epsilon, seeds, and the complete class prompts, are not supplied.

There are serious reproducibility inconsistencies. The stated Qwen3 30B-A3B citation describes Qwen3 rather than a clearly identified vision-language checkpoint, although the method requires image input. The supplement also claims Wan2.2 used 95,776 MiB on a single 'RTX 6000 Ada 100 GB'; RTX 6000 Ada hardware has 48 GB, so this configuration is not credible as written. No code or generated-data release is indicated.

The evidence for the proposed diagnosis and remedy is thin. The 'magnitude bias' motivation is supported only by two mean feature norms, with no variance, distribution, significance test, or demonstration that high norms actually determine MIL selections. Moreover, aligning real and synthetic normal features does not directly establish alignment between synthetic and real anomalies. The use of real-anomaly features for this analysis also needs a clear statement about whether they influenced method or hyperparameter development.

Generation quality is evaluated only on ShanghaiTech and apparently against unspecified 'real videos.' The paper must state whether those references are real abnormal training/test videos; using them for metric selection or development could undermine the anomaly-free premise. FID/FVD do not establish that generated clips depict the intended anomaly, and there is no human evaluation, semantic success rate, diversity/coverage analysis, or per-class fidelity assessment.

The most relevant pseudo-anomaly approaches cited in the related work are not included in the quantitative comparison. There is also no controlled normal-only UR-DMU baseline, random-seed baseline, raw-class-prompt baseline across both datasets, or alternative generator experiment. Consequently, it is difficult to isolate whether performance comes from CA-PAG, category-name supervision, Wan2.2's prior, DARM, or implementation choices.

The framing alternates between weakly supervised and unsupervised training without defining the new supervision regime precisely. The paper would be stronger as a concept/feasibility or applied-systems contribution, with appropriately qualified benchmark claims; under the default Algorithms/General standard, the missing controls and incomplete technical specification are consequential.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: reducing dependence on scarce, sensitive real anomaly footage. The combination of class-aware image retrieval, prompt refinement, video diffusion, and detector training is coherent and potentially useful.

The study reports results on two established datasets and includes component ablations, a synthetic-data scaling experiment, qualitative examples, generation metrics, computational cost, and a candid synthesis failure case.

The reported performance is promising within the authors' implementation: DARM improves the pseudo-trained UR-DMU baseline from 96.0% to 98.2% AUC on ShanghaiTech and from 80.2% to 82.5% on UCF-Crime.
The supplementary material provides useful generation settings and loss hyperparameters, and the paper is generally easy to follow.
weaknesses: Assuming the undeclared contribution type is Algorithms/General, the experimental comparisons do not establish the central claims reliably. On ShanghaiTech, the paper evaluates using the revised weakly supervised split but compares against UVAD numbers normally reported under the original normal-only protocol. Calling the UVAD comparison 'fully fair' is therefore insufficiently justified and potentially apples-to-oranges; this directly undermines the headline 98.2% result.

The method is not under the same information constraint as conventional UVAD. It receives the exact anomaly class names expected at inference and uses large pretrained CLIP, VLM, and video-generation models capable of encoding anomalous visual concepts. Thus, 'unsupervised' and 'no real abnormal data' are technically narrow descriptions, and the claimed collection-cost advantage does not justify treating class-informed synthetic supervision as directly comparable to ordinary normal-only UVAD.

The evidence for the proposed magnitude-bias mechanism is very weak. It consists mainly of one mean feature-norm comparison (23.03 versus 20.52), without distributions, variance, significance, class breakdown, or a demonstrated causal relationship with MIL errors. Moreover, the assignment in Eq. 10 explicitly normalizes features, while domain alignment operates only between real-normal and pseudo-normal streams rather than aligning pseudo anomalies with real anomalies. It is therefore unclear how the proposed losses specifically correct the claimed pseudo-anomaly magnitude shift.

The pseudo-normal stream is essential to the domain-alignment loss, yet its generation procedure, prompts, selection policy, and quality are not described. This makes a central part of DARM difficult to interpret or reproduce.

Equation 13 is underspecified and potentially unstable: the responsibility-weighted center divides by slot responsibility without an epsilon, while the outer weight can become very large for unused slots. The paper does not state whether Q or the centers are stop-gradient targets, how empty slots are handled, or whether memory parameters are updated by gradients or a separate rule. Calling this an 'update rule' obscures these important implementation details.

The ablations do not isolate several claimed contributions. There is no random-initial-image baseline to validate CLIP selection, no controlled comparison with fixed/manual prompts, no alternative or simpler generator, and no simple detector regularizer that could test whether DARM is necessary. Results are reported without multiple seeds or uncertainty, so gains as small as 0.5–1.1 AUC cannot be assessed for reliability.

Generation evaluation is incomplete. FID/FVD/KID/KVD are reported only on ShanghaiTech, with no clear specification of which real distribution is used, sample counts, or uncertainty. Computing or selecting against real abnormal test data would create a leakage concern, but the manuscript does not clearly state whether prompts, generator settings, or hyperparameters were fixed without examining those data. Absolute generation scores also lack comparison to other synthesis methods.

Only aggregate frame-level AUC is reported. Per-class performance, precision-recall metrics, robustness across scenes, and tests on anomaly classes not named during synthesis are absent. These evaluations are particularly important because the approach may learn the supplied category vocabulary rather than general anomaly detection, and the supplement acknowledges that some generated clips contain no actual anomaly.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the supplementary details: code and generated data are not provided; only example retrieval queries and prompts are shown; scene balancing is described as optional without saying whether it was used; and important training details such as epochs, seeds, checkpoint selection, exact feature pipeline, and complete prompts are missing.

The paper overstates practicality. Generation requires roughly 96 GB of GPU memory and 30–55 hours for relatively small synthetic sets, while possible generator bias, memorization of anomalous training content, surveillance/privacy implications, and failure modes from unrealistic or mislabeled generated clips receive little discussion.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in video anomaly detection: obtaining rare, sensitive, and costly abnormal footage. Training without real abnormal videos is a meaningful and potentially impactful objective.

The proposed pipeline is coherent: CLIP-based seed selection, VLM-based prompt refinement, image-to-video diffusion, and a detector adapted to synthetic-data artifacts form a sensible end-to-end approach.

The empirical results are promising. PA-VAD reports 98.2% frame-level AUC on ShanghaiTech and 82.5% on UCF-Crime without real abnormal training videos, substantially exceeding the listed normal-only baselines and approaching several methods trained with real anomalies.

The component ablations support the main design choices. Prompt refinement improves ShanghaiTech AUC from 94.9% to 96.0%, the usage-aware update produces a large gain, and combining both DARM components reaches 98.2%. Performance also scales reasonably with the number of generated clips.

The paper evaluates generation quality with both spatial and temporal distribution metrics and provides qualitative successes, a failure case, detector traces, generation costs, and dataset-specific hyperparameters. The presentation is generally clear and visually effective.
The stated limitation concerning long-horizon, context-dependent anomalies is appropriate and consistent with the weaker relative result on UCF-Crime.
weaknesses: The fairness of the headline comparisons is not established sufficiently. The paper evaluates ShanghaiTech using the revised weakly supervised split while several listed UVAD results appear to come from their customary protocol; the claim that comparison to UVAD is “fully fair” requires confirmation that test sets, preprocessing, features, and evaluation code are identical. Re-running representative baselines under the exact PA-VAD protocol would materially strengthen the case.

The strongest results lack repeated-run statistics, confidence intervals, or significance testing. This is important because the claimed advantage over the best real-abnormal ShanghaiTech baseline is only 0.6 AUC points and training includes stochastic video generation and MIL optimization.

The experimental analysis is concentrated on ShanghaiTech. The detailed CA-PAG/DARM ablations, pseudo-data scaling study, and generation-quality table are not reported for UCF-Crime, where synthesis is more difficult and the approach's limitations are most relevant.

The pseudo-normal videos required by the domain-alignment loss are not described with enough precision: their prompts, seed selection, filtering, and generation procedure are unclear. This is a significant reproducibility gap because these videos are central to DARM.

The causal justification for DARM is incomplete. The paper attributes its gains to correction of inflated pseudo-anomaly feature magnitudes, but it aligns real and synthetic normal streams rather than directly aligning pseudo and real anomalies, and it does not report post-DARM feature norms, domain discrepancy, memory-slot utilization, or MIL selection statistics. Thus the mechanism is plausible but not demonstrated.

CA-PAG is not compared against random seed-image selection, template-only prompts, alternative generators, or prior pseudo-anomaly generation methods. FID/FVD improvements from prompt refinement alone do not establish that the full generator is superior, and these distribution metrics do not directly measure whether the requested abnormal event is actually present.

The method assumes that all anomaly class names expected at inference time are known. This is stronger supervision than standard normal-only UVAD and limits claims of equivalence to that setting; evaluation on unseen anomaly categories or a clear closed-set qualification is needed.

Several implementation details remain underspecified, including the exact UR-DMU loss/configuration, discriminator architecture, feature pipeline used by the detector, slot-center handling when assignment mass is near zero, generation seeds, and release plans for generated clips/code. The very high approximately 96 GB generation-memory requirement also weakens the claim of broadly practical deployment.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: training video-anomaly detectors without collecting real abnormal footage. The pseudo-only setting is clearly defined and potentially impactful. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/ab6ee7fda7694e43a67e9cb445990f29/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

CA-PAG is a sensible, practical synthesis pipeline combining CLIP-based seed selection, VLM prompt refinement, and image-to-video diffusion. The substantial ShanghaiTech gains from seed selection and prompt refinement support these design choices.

The identification of a pseudo-induced feature-magnitude shortcut is interesting. Measurements before and after DARM, together with component ablations, provide useful empirical evidence that this issue affects MIL training.
The evaluation covers three established datasets. Under the authors' controlled pseudo-only configurations, DARM consistently improves the Qwen2.5-VL/UR-DMU baseline by 2.2–2.6 AUC points.

The paper includes useful analyses of generated-data quantity, open-set performance, generation costs, qualitative failures, and known difficulty with long-horizon anomalies. The presentation is generally clear and the main method is easy to follow.
weaknesses: The headline comparisons with real-abnormal methods are not adequately controlled. PA-VAD uses Qwen2.5-VL features, whereas major baselines use I3D, C3D, InternVL2, or no frozen clip-level backbone, and their numbers are copied from prior papers. Consequently, claims that pseudo-only training surpasses real-abnormal training are confounded by backbone, implementation, augmentation, and training-pipeline differences. A Real/Real counterpart using the same Qwen features, detector, and evaluation code is essential.

The evidence lacks statistical robustness. Main benchmark and ablation results are reported as single values despite stochastic video generation and training; only the open-set experiments include deviations. Multiple seeds, confidence intervals, and significance tests are particularly important for the small claimed margins over Real/Real baselines.

The open-set comparison may not be directly comparable: PA-VAD is averaged over three random class splits, while OpenVAD and RTFM values are quoted from their papers. The manuscript does not establish that identical held-out classes, splits, features, or training conditions were used. No class-agnostic or cross-dataset transfer experiment is provided.

Important reproduction details are missing or ambiguous. The construction of the pseudo-normal videos used by domain alignment is not described; the scene-balancing exponent and several retrieval parameters are unspecified; complete class prompts, seeds, and generated training lists are absent. The supplement says it provides the full Chinese refinement instruction, but only an English example is visible. No code or generated-data release commitment is stated.

The generation-quality evaluation is weak. FID/FVD/KID/KVD are reported only on ShanghaiTech without defining the real reference set, sample counts, or implementation details, and these distributional metrics do not establish that the requested anomalous event was generated correctly. The explanation that KID is unchanged because the settings have identical image statistics is also difficult to reconcile with the changed prompts and improved FID.

The mechanism behind DARM is not fully established. Domain alignment operates only between real-normal and pseudo-normal features even though the diagnosed shortcut concerns pseudo-abnormal features. The usage-weighted prototype loss then produces an exceptionally large norm reduction, but the paper does not rule out simple feature/prototype normalization, clipping, balanced assignment, or other regularizers as explanations. Comparisons to such simpler controls and sensitivity analyses for the new loss are needed.

The novelty of the individual ingredients is moderate: CLIP retrieval, VLM prompt rewriting, image-to-video generation, DANN alignment, and memory regularization are established ideas. The integration is useful, but stronger controlled evidence is needed to demonstrate that the proposed formulation, rather than pretrained-model strength or implementation choices, causes the reported advantage.

The practical framing is somewhat overstated. Training assumes prior knowledge of the benchmark's abnormal class names and uses a 14B video generator on two 96-GB GPUs, with up to roughly 55 hours of synthesis. The paper should more clearly delimit this supervision and compute tradeoff and discuss surveillance-related misuse, demographic bias, and failures on subtle anomalies. Overall, the idea is promising, but the comparison and reproducibility gaps leave a slight preference for rejection in its current form.

strengths: The pseudo-only training objective addresses a meaningful practical problem: reducing dependence on scarce, sensitive real abnormal footage. Combining class-aware seed retrieval, prompt refinement, video diffusion, and anomaly detection is potentially useful.

The manuscript identifies an interesting empirical phenomenon: pseudo anomalies can develop substantially inflated feature norms inside the MIL detector. Results are reported across three established VAD benchmarks and multiple frozen feature spaces.

The component ablations are reasonably extensive. On ShanghaiTech, initial-image retrieval, prompt refinement, domain alignment, and the usage-aware update are evaluated separately; the paper also varies the number of generated clips and reports generation costs and representative failure cases.

The reported detection results are strong, particularly 98.2% AUC on ShanghaiTech and 95.1% on XD-Violence. The inclusion of open-set experiments, generation-quality metrics, qualitative score traces, and some standard deviations broadens the empirical evaluation.

The paper is generally readable, and it appropriately acknowledges that class names and large pretrained generative/vision-language models constitute stronger prior knowledge than conventional normal-only UVAD.
weaknesses: The central state-of-the-art comparisons are not controlled. PA-VAD uses Qwen2.5-VL features, whereas the highlighted real-abnormal baselines use I3D, C3D, or other representations. There is no matched Real/Real UR-DMU or normal-only baseline using the same Qwen features, detector, preprocessing, and training budget. Consequently, the claims that pseudo-only training surpasses methods trained on real anomalies cannot be attributed to CA-PAG or DARM.

The paper calls the regime “unsupervised,” but generation requires the benchmark’s abnormal class taxonomy and powerful pretrained models that may encode abnormal-event knowledge. This is materially different from normal-only UVAD. The method remains valuable as class-informed synthetic supervision, but the protocol and comparisons should be framed accordingly.

The evidence for the proposed mechanism is incomplete. Domain alignment operates only between real-normal and pseudo-normal streams, while the claimed problem concerns pseudo-abnormal versus real-abnormal features. The usage-aware loss does not explicitly constrain feature norms, yet it is credited with reducing detector-space norms by more than an order of magnitude. Comparisons against simple feature normalization, norm penalties, entropy/balancing regularizers, and matched memory-update alternatives are missing.

The open-set experiment does not convincingly demonstrate unseen-class detection. It evaluates on the full test set containing both seen and held-out classes, so gains may be driven by seen categories. Unseen-only results, per-class results, identical class splits for all methods, and matched reruns of baselines are needed. Comparing the authors’ three-split averages against numbers quoted from prior papers is insufficient for strong conclusions.

Main benchmark results appear to be single runs, despite several claimed improvements over prior work being below one AUC point. There are no variances, significance tests, or matched reruns for the primary tables, making it difficult to judge whether the reported margins are robust.

The generation evaluation is underspecified: the real-video reference set for FID/FVD/KID/KVD is not identified, raising questions about whether abnormal test footage was inspected or used during development. These metrics are also estimated from small generated sets without uncertainty. The explanation that KID is unchanged because both settings have “identical image statistics” is unsupported because prompt refinement generates different output frames.

Reproducibility is insufficient. Important details such as complete per-class prompts and negative phrases, retrieval K, scene-balancing exponent, retrieval weight, assignment temperature, epsilon, seed selection, random seeds, and exact pseudo-normal generation procedure are absent or incomplete. The supplement says the full original Chinese VLM instruction is provided, but only an English example is visible.

The usage-aware objective has unresolved technical issues: the responsibility-weighted center divides by potentially tiny slot usage without an explicit stabilizer, and aggressively weighting low-usage slots can amplify noisy assignments. No stability analysis, convergence evidence, or sensitivity study is supplied.

Evaluation is limited to a single video generator and largely one detector backbone. The qualitative evidence is selectively presented, while the acknowledged failures on subtle and long-horizon events are not quantified by anomaly class. This weakens the broader scalability and generality claims.

The practical discussion understates substantial generation requirements—roughly 18–55 hours on two high-memory GPUs—and does not examine surveillance bias, privacy implications of source normal footage, or misuse risks from synthesizing violent/criminal content. These omissions matter for the deployment motivation.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important VAD setting: training without real abnormal footage. CA-PAG combines class-aware normal-frame retrieval, VLM prompt refinement, and video diffusion to produce anomaly supervision, while DARM targets a clearly identified failure mode of pseudo-only MIL training. This forms a coherent Algorithms/General contribution with potential impact where abnormal footage is rare, sensitive, or expensive.

The empirical results are promising and broad: PA-VAD reports 98.2% AUC on ShanghaiTech, 82.5% on UCF-Crime, and 95.1% on XD-Violence, with consistent improvements over the unregularized UR-DMU-based variant on all three datasets. Performance saturating around 140 generated clips also suggests reasonable data efficiency.

The ablations provide useful evidence for both sides of the framework. On ShanghaiTech, class-aware seed selection improves AUC from 86.7% to 94.9%, prompt refinement raises it to 96.0%, and the complete DARM reaches 98.2%. The feature-norm analysis is especially interesting: it exposes a substantial pseudo-anomaly magnitude shortcut inside the detector and shows that full DARM largely closes this gap.

The open-set experiments are valuable because they directly test a central risk of class-conditioned pseudo generation. Gains over OpenVAD on both Crime and XD, including the one-seen-class setting, support transfer beyond the generated category set. The paper also candidly presents a generation failure case and acknowledges limitations for long-horizon, context-heavy anomalies.

The manuscript is generally clear and visually well organized, with equations, qualitative score traces, generation examples, hyperparameters, and computational-cost reporting that make the overall approach understandable. weaknesses: The headline comparisons are not well controlled. PA-VAD uses 3,584-dimensional Qwen2.5-VL features and several powerful pretrained models, whereas most quoted UVAD/WVAD results use I3D, C3D, or method-specific representations. Because results are quoted from prior papers rather than reproduced under a shared backbone and training pipeline, the claims of surpassing real-abnormal methods cannot be cleanly attributed to pseudo-only training or DARM. Same-backbone comparisons against normal-only and real-abnormal baselines are needed.

The paper calls the regime “unsupervised,” but it requires the benchmark's abnormal class names and uses large pretrained CLIP, VLM, and diffusion priors that may encode abnormal-event knowledge. This is still a useful class-informed, pseudo-supervised setting, but it is not directly equivalent to conventional normal-only UVAD; the terminology and comparisons should be qualified more consistently.

Reproducibility remains incomplete. The construction of the pseudo-normal videos used by domain alignment is not explained. Important CA-PAG details such as K, the negative-query aggregation, lambda in Eq. 4, the scene-balancing exponent and budgets, candidate-frame sampling, and full prompts are missing or ambiguous; the supplement says the full Chinese refinement prompt is provided but only presents an English example. Training duration, MIL Top-k settings, and random seeds are also absent.

The evidence lacks uncertainty for the principal closed-set results despite stochastic video generation and very small generated sets. Component ablations are concentrated on ShanghaiTech, generation-quality metrics are reported only there, and no sensitivity analysis is given for DARM coefficients or memory-bank size. Multiple generation/training seeds and ablations on Crime and XD would make the 0.6–0.9 point superiority claims substantially more convincing.

Some analyses do not fully establish the proposed mechanism. Domain alignment operates on real-normal versus pseudo-normal features, while the claimed problem concerns pseudo-abnormal magnitude; the large norm correction is mainly associated with the usage-aware update, but there is no comparison to simpler feature normalization, norm clipping, prototype balancing, or direct norm regularization. The reported detector-space norm changes are therefore suggestive rather than causal evidence that the proposed formulation is necessary.

The generation evaluation is underspecified: it is unclear which real-video distribution, sample counts, preprocessing, and metric implementation are used. The explanation that unchanged KID means the two generation settings have “identical image statistics” is not justified, because prompt refinement changes the generated frames. There is also no direct quality comparison with alternative pseudo-anomaly generators.

Open-set comparability needs clarification. PA-VAD averages three random class splits, while prior values are quoted from their papers; the manuscript should verify identical class partitions and report performance specifically on held-out anomaly frames rather than only AUC over a full test set containing both seen and unseen classes.
